job.style: a passage that starts from a common wrong idea and corrects it

passage: Many people mistakenly believe that Artificial Intelligence is just a computer program that knows everything or feels emotions like a human. In reality, AI is a tool designed to perform specific tasks by learning patterns from large amounts of data, rather than following a fixed list of pre-written instructions. For instance, an AI trained to play chess is an expert at that game, but it cannot automatically drive a car or write a story because its intelligence is limited to its training. Furthermore, because AI learns from data provided by humans, it can inherit the biases present in that information. This means that if the training data is flawed, the AI’s decisions might be unfair or incorrect. We must also remember that a chatbot is simply predicting the next likely word in a sentence based on its training; it does not 'know' facts or have feelings. Even if a chatbot sounds confident and writes perfectly, it can still provide wrong information. Therefore, we should always verify important facts rather than assuming an AI is always right just because it sounds professional or because multiple bots give the same answer.

items.evidence: For instance, an AI trained to play chess is an expert at that game, but it cannot automatically drive a car or write a story because its intelligence is limited to its training.
items.q: An AI beats every person at chess. What will happen if it is asked to drive a car?
options: It will struggle, as it learned only one game
It will drive well, as it is very smart
It will drive well once all answers are typed in
It will drive well, as it has a human-like body
items.explain: An AI's intelligence is limited to its training, so a chess AI cannot automatically drive a car.

wrong.why: thinks skill at chess means skill at everything
thinks programmers type in every answer
thinks AI is a human-like robot

items.evidence: Furthermore, because AI learns from data provided by humans, it can inherit the biases present in that information.
items.q: A fair-minded programmer builds an AI, but it treats some people unfairly. Which explains this?
options: It picked up unfair patterns from its data
The programmer secretly wanted it to be unfair
It formed its own opinions about those people
It was never shown any examples to learn from
items.explain: AI learns from data given by humans, so it can take on the biases in that data.

wrong.why: thinks bias only comes from a deliberately unfair programmer
thinks AI has its own feelings and opinions
thinks AI can learn without examples

items.evidence: We must also remember that a chatbot is simply predicting the next likely word in a sentence based on its training; it does not 'know' facts or have feelings.
items.q: Ravi is rude to a chatbot and it replies, 'Sorry, I feel sad.' What is really happening?
options: It is guessing likely words from its training
It is truly sad after being treated rudely
It is reading a reply typed in for rudeness
It is recalling facts it knows about Ravi
items.explain: A chatbot only predicts the next likely word; it has no feelings and does not know facts.

wrong.why: thinks chatbots feel hurt when scolded
thinks every reply was pre-written by programmers
thinks the chatbot really knows facts

items.evidence: Therefore, we should always verify important facts rather than assuming an AI is always right just because it sounds professional or because multiple bots give the same answer.
items.q: Two chatbots give Meena the same confident answer for her project. What should she do next?
options: She should check it in a reliable source
She should use it, since both bots agree
She should use it, as it sounds so sure
She should use it, as computers cannot be biased
items.explain: Even confident or matching AI answers can be wrong, so important facts must always be verified.

wrong.why: thinks two matching bots must be right
thinks a confident answer must be correct
thinks computers are always fair and right
